context: four shops · press, body, paint and assembly; paint shop is the longest and start of production is fixed

brief.intro: New to this project type? A car plant is four factories in a row. The press shop stamps steel coil into body panels on huge presses. The body shop welds the panels into a body shell with hundreds of robots. The paint shop cleans, dips, seals, sprays and bakes the body in a very clean, tightly controlled building. Final assembly then fits everything else — engine or battery, interior, wheels — on a moving line and tests the finished car. The four shops are linked by conveyors and fed by an energy centre. The start-of-production date is fixed years ahead with the vehicle launch, so the plan is built backwards from it. The paint shop, with its process equipment, ovens, air-handling and environmental permits, is nearly always the longest path, and the press foundations are the heaviest civil item.

scope.name: Site preparation & enabling
scope.desc: Grading, access roads, temporary facilities and underground services.

scope.name: Building & machine foundations
scope.desc: Column footings plus the heavy bases, pits and trenches the machines sit on — set out from the equipment drawings.

scope.name: Steel structure & envelope
scope.desc: Portal frames, crane beams, roof and wall cladding, making the hall weather-tight.

scope.name: Industrial floor
scope.desc: Flat, hard-wearing floor slab, cast after the roof is on and before the machines move in.

scope.name: Press shop
scope.desc: Coil handling, blanking and press lines on deep foundations, die storage.

scope.name: Body shop
scope.desc: Robotic welding cells, framing stations and body storage.

scope.name: Paint shop
scope.desc: Pre-treatment and e-coat tanks, sealer, spray booths, ovens and air-supply units.

scope.name: Final assembly
scope.desc: Trim, chassis and final lines, marriage station, fluid filling.

scope.name: End-of-line test & finish
scope.desc: Wheel alignment, roller test, water test and inspection.

scope.name: Conveyors & logistics
scope.desc: Skid and overhead conveyors between shops, parts supermarket and docks.

scope.name: Energy centre
scope.desc: Compressed air, chilled and hot water, gas and power distribution.

scope.name: Plant utilities
scope.desc: Compressed air, Chilled & hot water, Natural gas, Demineralised water & effluent treatment — the services every machine needs before it can run.

scope.name: Power supply & control
scope.desc: Substation, transformers, switchgear, cabling and the plant control system.

scope.name: Fire protection, HVAC & dust / fume extraction
scope.desc: Life-safety and environmental systems required for the operating permit.

scope.name: Commissioning & ramp-up
scope.desc: Equipment try-outs, pre-series cars, quality gates, then start of production and a ramp-up curve to full rate.

glossary.term: Press shop / body shop / paint shop / assembly
glossary.plain: the four production stages of a car plant.
the welded steel body shell before paint.
the first, electrically deposited paint layer, applied by dipping the whole body in a tank.
regenerative thermal oxidiser — burns the solvent fumes from the ovens and booths.
the station where the body is joined to the powertrain and chassis.
the time between two cars leaving the line; all stations are designed to it.
trial cars built before the official start to prove the process and train the staff.
start of production — the contractual date of the first saleable car.

must_get_right: Plan backwards from the start-of-production date; it is tied to the vehicle launch and does not move.
The paint shop is the longest chain — process design, permits (emissions, effluent), building, equipment, cleanliness, first paint — and should start first.
Press foundations are deep, heavy and need the press maker's loads early; they often start before the building steel.
Each shop is handed to the equipment suppliers on a 'building ready' date (roof tight, floor finished, power available). Fix those dates shop by shop and protect them.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: For each shop: design freeze → foundations and pits → steel → roof and cladding → floor → building ready → equipment installation → power and utilities → try-out. Shops then join through the conveyors: first panels → first bodies → first painted bodies → pre-series → SOP. The critical path normally runs through the paint shop.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late vehicle design changes, paint-shop permits and cleanliness, press delivery, building-ready dates slipping into installation, and quality problems during pre-series. Contingency is held before pre-series and before SOP.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
